summary:
Cyprus does not criminalise same-sex sexual activity. Consensual conduct was decriminalised in 1998 after the European Court of Human Rights held in Modinos v. Cyprus that Criminal Code section 171 violated the right to private life. The offence of promoting homosexuality was lifted in 2000 and unequal ages of consent were equalised in 2002. The universal age of consent is now 17. The former military exclusion of homosexuals has been removed. In the northern part of the island, deputies voted on 27 January 2014 to repeal the provision that punished homosexual acts with up to five years’ imprisonment.

Cypriot law provides no general prohibition of discrimination based on gender identity. The 2004 Equal Treatment in Employment and Occupation Law prohibits only sexual-orientation discrimination in employment. Gender identity remains absent from equal-treatment grounds.

Article 99 of the Penal Code, titled incitement to violence or hatred due to sexual orientation or gender identity, punishes intentional public threatening, insulting or offensive urging or incitement, orally or in writing, of violence or hatred on those grounds with imprisonment not exceeding three years or a fine. The provision originated in the October 2013 Penal Code amendment and was carried into Law 87(I)/2015 as a public hate-speech offence. Parliament raised the fine for sexual-orientation or gender-identity hate speech in October 2024 to 10,000 euros. Separate 2017 provisions are reported as punishing incitement based on sexual orientation with up to five years’ imprisonment and a fine up to 10,000 euros.

Law 31(I)/2017 provides that prejudice-based motivation operates as an aggravating factor in sentencing.

Enforcement of hate-crime protection is inconsistent. Eleven complaints were examined in 2015 with five criminal prosecutions reported as pending trial. Reports of incitement against LGBT people have at times resulted in no police or legal action, most notably when committed by clergy of the Greek Orthodox Church. Police failed to establish a hate-crime motive after a February 2019 attack on a gay man in Nicosia, and no police action was reported after a second Nicosia incident four months later. An LGBTI non-governmental organisation assessed the legislation as fragmented and inadequate, finding that many LGBTI persons remain not open about sexual orientation or gender identity and do not report homophobic violence or discrimination.

Conversion practices are banned and criminalised under Law 39(I)/2023, adopted by parliamentary vote on 25 May 2023.

No gender-recognition law is in force. The national report prepared for the Universal Periodic Review stated that legislation for correcting registered sex for adults and minors was in preparation and would require only a Registrar decision without prior medical intervention or psychiatric reports. A bill discussed after President Nicos Anastasiades met Accept-LGBT Cyprus in November 2017 would have allowed persons over 18 to change legal gender on the basis of self-determination without diagnosis, hormonal treatment or sex reassignment surgery. On 10 June 2019 four parents of transgender children urged speedy adoption after months of stalling and delay. The legal gender recognition bill was approved by the Council of Ministers in September 2022 with a first parliamentary reading in November 2022 and remained pending in 2024.

Queer Cyprus documents a separate recognition practice in the northern part of the island. That process is described as self-determination without psychiatric or surgical gatekeeping and as explicitly including recognition of non-binary identities.

Marriage remains legally recognised only as a union between one man and one woman, with no same-sex marriage recognition. A civil-union law granting several marriage rights and benefits passed on 26 November 2015 by 39 votes in favour, 12 against and 3 abstentions and took effect on 9 December 2015. Adoption remains reserved to heterosexual couples only.
tangentialFactors:
Cyprus accepted all eight SOGIESC recommendations recorded in the ILGA report on the 32nd Universal Periodic Review working group session of 29 January 2019. A separate account of the 2019 review records acceptance of all seven LGBT-related recommendations, which included combating discrimination and violence, criminalising harassment, adopting an action plan against homophobia and transphobia, and adopting a gender recognition law. The European Commission against Racism and Intolerance had urged inclusion of gender identity as a prohibited discrimination ground. Cyprus joined the Equal Rights Coalition as its 40th member in August 2018.

State reporting presented hate-speech legislation as delivered while a gender-identity discrimination ground and trans legislation remained undelivered. No anti-homophobia action plan exists.

In 2017 the Ministry of Education established the HOMBAT programme on combating homophobic and transphobic bullying at schools to train teachers and professors on bullying and harassment directed at LGBT students.

Prison guards received two days of LGBTI+ training in April 2023 after anti-LGBTI harassment complaints to the Ombudswoman.
localsOnly:
For 2017, antidiscrimination coverage was formally described as extending to employment, social protection, social insurance, social benefits, health care, education, union and professional-organisation participation and access to goods and services on sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds. The LGBTI assessment found housing benefits favouring traditional families within that framework.

Queer Cyprus operates a confidential psychosocial and legal support line seven days per week covering identity, work, family, shelter, health and military-service issues.
outOfScopeNotes:
The legislative status of the gender-recognition bill after 2024 is not sourced in the inventory. Later enforcement totals beyond the 2015 complaint and prosecution figures and the 2019 Nicosia incidents are not sourced.

The precise relationship between Article 99 penalties and the separately reported 2017 incitement penalties of up to five years is unresolved on the sources provided.

Entry and visa rules, airport and border screening practice, and bathroom or facilities rules are not sourced in the inventory.
